name: Beanie Babies
blurb: Ty's small bean-filled plush animals, the subject of a late-1990s collecting bubble
title: Beanie Babies: The 1990s Craze and What They Are Worth Now
description: Beanie Babies are small plush animals made by Ty Inc. since 1994. They fuelled a collecting bubble that burst around 1999; most are worth a few dollars now.
h1: What were Beanie Babies, and are they worth anything?
answer: Beanie Babies are small plush animals stuffed with plastic pellets, made by Ty Warner's company Ty Inc. and first sold for about $5 in 1994. Ty limited supply and "retired" characters, which turned them into a collecting frenzy in the late 1990s, with some resold for thousands. The bubble burst around 1999–2000; most Beanie Babies today sell for a few dollars, though Ty still makes them.

body: A Beanie Baby is a palm-sized animal filled loosely with plastic pellets rather than packed with stuffing, so it slumps and can be posed. Each one has a name and a little poem on its heart-shaped Ty swing tag. Collectors kept the tags on, often in plastic protectors, because a missing or creased tag lowered resale value.

Ty Warner unveiled the line at the 1993 Toy Fair in New York, and the first ones went on sale in Chicago in 1994. The Original Nine were Legs the Frog, Squealer the Pig, Spot the Dog, Flash the Dolphin, Splash the Whale, Chocolate the Moose, Patti the Platypus, Brownie the Bear (later renamed Cubbie) and Pinchers the Lobster.

sections.h: How the bubble grew and burst

head: Year
What happened
rows: First Beanie Babies sold in Chicago for about $5
Ty caps orders at 36 of each character per store per month and starts "retiring" characters
McDonald's Teenie Beanie Babies Happy Meal giveaway; about 100 million go in around ten days
Beanies are resold for many times retail and make up about 10% of eBay's sales
Ty announces all Beanies will be retired at the end of the year and releases a black bear called The End
After a public vote, about 90% choose to continue; production goes on with a bear called The Beginning

body: Scarcity was the engine. Shops could not get as many as they wanted, retired characters became instantly harder to find, and price guides and online auctions told owners their toys were investments. But Ty had made enormous numbers, and when the novelty faded there were simply too many of each one for prices to hold.

sections.h: Are Beanie Babies worth anything now?
body: For almost everyone, no. Most Beanie Babies now sell for a few dollars, including famous names like Princess the bear, which was produced in large numbers. Listings asking tens of thousands of dollars are asking prices, not sales.

A small number of genuine rarities still attract collectors, such as early versions with tag errors and the royal blue Peanut the elephant, made briefly before Ty changed its color. Even these depend on authentication, tags and condition.
Yes. Ty never stopped after the 2000 vote and still sells new Beanie Babies. The original 1990s characters are only found second-hand.

faq.a: Ty Inc., the toy company Ty Warner founded in 1986. He introduced Beanie Babies at the 1993 New York Toy Fair.

faq.q: Why did the Beanie Baby bubble burst?
faq.a: Value rested on scarcity, but Ty made huge numbers. When demand faded and the 1999 retirement announcement was reversed, many collectors felt let down and resale prices fell.

faq.q: Is the Princess Diana bear valuable?
faq.a: Generally not. Princess was made in large numbers, and ordinary examples sell cheaply; very high prices online are usually asking prices that never sell.
